q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Contribution" is:
e: 'Ansha' means a share or part, so Anshadan is the share paid towards a common fund or cost. Anudan is a grant, Daan a donation and Shulk a fee.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Recovery" is:
e: Vasuli means realising or collecting an amount due from a person. Katauti is a deduction from payment, Dhan Vapasi a refund and Samayojan an adjustment.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Refund" is:
e: Dhan Vapasi literally means 'return of money', i.e., paying back an amount already received. Vasuli is recovery of dues and Bakaya denotes arrears, not a refund.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Adjustment" is:
e: Samayojan means setting off or adjusting one amount against another in the accounts. Sanshodhan is an amendment, Samanvay is coordination and Samadhan is a solution.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Arrears" is:
e: Bakaya denotes the amount that remains due and unpaid, i.e., arrears. Rin is a loan or debt, Shesh is the remainder and Dhan Vapasi is a refund.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Nomination" is:
e: Namankan is the act of naming a person for something, as a nominee or candidate. Niyukti is appointment, Chayan is selection and Panjikaran is registration.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Insurance" is:
e: Bima is the established official term for insurance, the cover taken against risk. Suraksha means protection in general, Jama a deposit and Garanti a guarantee.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Form" (printed form) is:
e: Prapatra is the prescribed printed form used for applications and records. Namuna is a specimen or sample, Aavedan Patra an application form and Praroop a draft or format.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Initials" is:
e: Initials are shortened signatures, hence Laghu (short) Hastakshar. Hastakshar alone is the full signature, Mudra is a seal or stamp and Angutha Nishan a thumb impression.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Scale of Pay" is:
e: Vetanman is the graded scale of pay attached to a post, running from minimum to maximum. Mool Vetan is only the basic pay and Vetan Vriddhi is an increment.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Basic Pay" is:
e: 'Mool' means the base, so Mool Vetan is the pay drawn in the pay scale excluding allowances. Vetanman is the scale itself and Parilabdhiyan are total emoluments.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Emoluments" is:
e: Parilabdhiyan is the collective term for everything an employee receives - pay, allowances and other benefits. Vetan is pay alone and Bhatte are only the allowances.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Posting" is:
e: Tainati means posting or stationing an employee at a place of duty. Niyukti is appointment, Sthanantaran is transfer and Pratiniyukti is deputation.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Proposal" is:
e: Prastav is a proposal formally put up for consideration or approval. Aavedan is an application, Anurodh a request and Sankalp a resolution.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "House Rent Allowance" is:
e: The term combines all three elements of the English term - Makan (house), Kiraya (rent) and Bhatta (allowance); the other options each drop one element.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Clerk" is:
e: Lipik, derived from 'Lipi' meaning script or writing, is the official who does clerical work. Lekhak is an author or writer, and Sahayak an assistant.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Assistant" is:
e: Sahayak literally means a helper, which matches the role of an Assistant. Prabhari is the officer in charge, Nirikshak an inspector and Adhinasth a subordinate.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Under Secretary" is:
e: In the secretariat hierarchy 'Avar' denotes the under or junior level, so Under Secretary is Avar Sachiv. Up Sachiv is Deputy Secretary and Sanyukt Sachiv is Joint Secretary.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Gazetted Officer" is:
e: A gazetted officer is one whose appointment is notified in the official Gazette, the Rajpatra; hence he is called Rajpatrit Adhikari, a gazette-notified officer.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Administration" is:
e: Prashasan is the standard term for administration, the machinery for running the government. Prabandhan is management, Sanchalan is conduct of operations and Niyaman is regulation.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Payment" is:
e: Bhugtan means making a payment or disbursement. Prapti is a receipt, Jama a deposit or credit, and Vasuli the recovery or collection of dues.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Division" (as in a Railway Division) is:
e: In railway and general administrative usage a Division is called Mandal. Khand is a section or part, Anchal a region and Prakoshth a cell or chamber.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "General Manager" is:
e: 'Maha' denotes the highest level, so the General Manager heading a railway zone is Mahaprabandhak. Mukhya Prabandhak is Chief Manager and Pradhan Prabandhak Principal Manager.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Workshop" is:
e: Karyashala - Karya (work) plus Shala (hall or place) - is where manufacturing and repair work is carried out. Prayogshala is a laboratory and Bhandar Griha a storehouse.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Maintenance" is:
e: Anurakshan means upkeep and preservation of assets in working condition. Marammat is only repair work, Sudhar Karya improvement work and Navikaran renewal.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Register" (a book of record) is:
e: A register, as a book of record, is Panji. Suchi is a list, Talika a table and Bahi a traditional account book or ledger.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Employee" is:
e: Karmachari is the general official term for a person employed in service. Sevak implies a servant or attendant, while Shramik and Mazdoor denote manual labourers.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Script" is:
e: Lipi is the system of written characters used for a language, i.e., its script. Akshar is a single letter, Varna a letter or sound unit, and Bhasha the language itself.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Contract" is:
e: Samvida is the legal term for a contract, an agreement enforceable by law. Theka is the colloquial word for a contract job, Nivida a tender and Samjhota a compromise.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Seminar" is:
e: Sangoshthi is a gathering for scholarly discussion, i.e., a seminar. Baithak and Sabha are ordinary meetings or assemblies, and Parisamvad is a dialogue or discussion.

q: The Fifth World Hindi Conference was held in the year 1996 at:
e: The World Hindi Conferences began at Nagpur in 1975; the fifth conference in the series was hosted in 1996 at Port of Spain, the capital of Trinidad and Tobago.

q: The Seventh World Hindi Conference was held in the year 2003 at:
e: The seventh World Hindi Conference was held in 2003 at Paramaribo, capital of Suriname, a country with a large Hindi-speaking population of Indian origin.

q: With the inclusion of Sindhi in the Eighth Schedule in the year 1967, the total number of languages included in the Schedule rose to:
e: The Eighth Schedule originally listed fourteen languages. Sindhi was added by the Constitution (Twenty-first Amendment) Act, 1967, raising the total number of scheduled languages to fifteen.

q: According to the Census of India, 2011, the sixth most widely spoken language (mother tongue) in India is:
e: In Census 2011 the order of mother tongues after Hindi is Bengali, Marathi, Telugu and Tamil; Gujarati comes next, at the sixth place, with Urdu seventh.

q: The official language of Bangladesh is:
e: Bengali (Bangla) is the official language of Bangladesh. The movement for its recognition in erstwhile East Pakistan is commemorated through International Mother Language Day.

q: The official language of Pakistan is:
e: Urdu is the national and official language of Pakistan, used for government and inter-provincial communication, although Punjabi is spoken by the largest share of its people.

q: The Sahitya Akademi, India's national academy of letters, was established in the year:
e: The Sahitya Akademi, India's national academy of letters, was established in 1954 to promote literature and literary activity in the Indian languages.

q: The Central Institute of Indian Languages, headquartered at Mysuru, was established in the year:
e: The Central Institute of Indian Languages at Mysuru was established in 1969 for the coordinated development of Indian languages and language research.

q: The Hindi Sahitya Sammelan, a leading organisation for the promotion of Hindi, was founded in the year:
e: The Hindi Sahitya Sammelan, a leading organisation for the promotion of Hindi, was founded in 1910; its headquarters is at Prayagraj.

q: International Mother Language Day is observed every year on:
e: International Mother Language Day is observed on 21 February, proclaimed by UNESCO in memory of the 1952 Dhaka movement for the Bengali language.

q: The first All India Progressive Writers' Conference, held at Lucknow in the year 1936, was presided over by:
e: Munshi Premchand presided over the first All India Progressive Writers' Conference held at Lucknow in 1936, where he delivered his famous presidential address on the purpose of literature.

q: 'Godan', regarded as one of the greatest novels in Hindi literature, was written by:
e: 'Godan', the classic novel of peasant life centred on the character Hori, is Munshi Premchand's most celebrated work and a landmark of Hindi fiction.

q: The celebrated Hindi poem 'Madhushala' was composed by:
e: 'Madhushala', the famous collection of quatrains built on the imagery of the tavern and wine, was composed by Harivansh Rai Bachchan.

q: 'Kamayani', the celebrated Hindi epic poem, was written by:
e: 'Kamayani', the modern epic poem on Manu, Shraddha and the deluge, is the masterpiece of Jaishankar Prasad, the leading figure of Chhayavad poetry.

q: 'Sursagar', a collection of devotional verses on Lord Krishna, was composed by:
e: 'Sursagar', the vast collection of devotional verses (pads) on the life and sports of Lord Krishna, is the celebrated work of the saint-poet Surdas.

q: 'Vinay Patrika', a collection of devotional hymns, was composed by:
e: 'Vinay Patrika', a collection of devotional hymns of humility and supplication addressed mainly to Lord Rama, was composed by Goswami Tulsidas.

q: 'Chandrakanta', the popular early Hindi novel, was written by:
e: 'Chandrakanta', the immensely popular early Hindi novel full of romance and tilismi wonders, was written by Devaki Nandan Khatri and drew countless readers to Hindi.

q: 'Maila Anchal', the celebrated Hindi novel depicting rural life in Bihar, was written by:
e: 'Maila Anchal', depicting rural life in the Purnea region of Bihar, is the landmark regional (anchalik) novel of Phanishwar Nath Renu.

q: 'Rashmirathi', the celebrated Hindi poem based on the life of Karna, was written by:
e: 'Rashmirathi', the celebrated long poem portraying the life and generosity of Karna of the Mahabharata, was written by Ramdhari Singh Dinkar.

q: Which of the following Hindi poets is popularly known as the 'Rashtrakavi' (national poet)?
e: Maithili Sharan Gupt, the pioneer of Khari Boli poetry and author of 'Bharat-Bharati', is honoured with the title of Rashtrakavi, the national poet.

q: Which Hindi poetess is popularly known as the 'Modern Meera'?
e: Mahadevi Varma, the great Chhayavad poetess whose verse is filled with devotion, longing and mysticism, is popularly called the 'Modern Meera'.

q: The first Hindi writer to receive the Jnanpith Award was:
e: Sumitranandan Pant received the Jnanpith Award for his poetry collection 'Chidambara', becoming the first Hindi writer to receive this highest literary honour.

q: The first recipient of the Jnanpith Award, in the year 1965, was:
e: The very first Jnanpith Award, given in 1965, went to G. Sankara Kurup, the celebrated Malayalam poet; Indian literature's highest honour thus began with Malayalam.

q: Modern Hindi has evolved from which of the following?
e: Modern Hindi (Khari Boli) developed through the Shauraseni Prakrit and Apabhramsha of the western region. Magadhi Apabhramsha gave rise to the eastern languages like Bengali and Odia.

q: The Awadhi dialect belongs to which group of Hindi dialects?
e: Awadhi, the language of the Ramcharitmanas region, belongs to the Eastern Hindi group, along with Bagheli and Chhattisgarhi.

q: The Bhojpuri language belongs to which group of languages/dialects?
e: Bhojpuri, together with Maithili and Magahi, forms the Bihari group of languages, which is distinct from both the Eastern Hindi and Western Hindi groups.

q: The Marwari dialect is a dialect of:
e: Marwari, spoken in the Marwar region of western Rajasthan, is a principal dialect of Rajasthani, along with Mewari, Dhundhari and Hadoti.

q: According to the Census of India, 2011, the number of persons who returned Hindi as their mother tongue was approximately:
e: Census 2011 recorded about 52.8 crore persons returning Hindi as their mother tongue - by far the largest number for any language in India.

q: Arabic became one of the official languages of the United Nations in the year:
e: Arabic was adopted as an official language of the United Nations in 1973, joining English, French, Spanish, Russian and Chinese as the sixth official language.

q: The court language of the Mughal emperors in India was:
e: Persian remained the language of the Mughal court and of administration in India for centuries, and official records and court business were conducted in it.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Leave" is:
e: Avakash is the official term for leave of absence as well as a holiday. Anumati is permission, Aavedan an application and Aadesh an order.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Government" is:
e: Sarkar is the standard Hindi equivalent of Government in administrative usage. Sansad is Parliament, Sangathan an organisation and Samiti a committee.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "President" is:
e: Rashtrapati, the head of the Rashtra (nation), is the President of India. Rajyapal is the Governor of a State and Pradhan Mantri the Prime Minister.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Prime Minister" is:
e: Pradhan Mantri literally means the chief minister of the Union, i.e., the Prime Minister. Mukhya Mantri is the Chief Minister of a State.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Governor" is:
e: Rajyapal is the Governor of a State, appointed by the President. Kulapati is the Vice-Chancellor of a university and Rashtrapati the President.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Court" is:
e: Nyayalaya, from Nyaya (justice) and Aalaya (abode), is a court of law. Sachivalaya is a secretariat and Mantralaya a ministry.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Affidavit" is:
e: An affidavit is a written statement made on oath, hence Shapath Patra, an oath document. Praman Patra is a certificate and Yachika a petition.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Petition" is:
e: Yachika is a formal petition, especially one presented to a court or authority. Aavedan Patra is an application and Adhisuchna a notification.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Reference" is:
e: Sandarbh means reference - the citation of an earlier letter, order or context. Sandesh is a message and Sankalp a resolution or resolve.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Acknowledgement" is:
e: Paavati is the slip or receipt given in acknowledgement of something received, such as a letter. Paripatra is a circular and Patravali a file of papers.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Copy" is:
e: Pratilipi is a copy or replica of a document. Praroop is a draft, Prapatra a form and Prishthankan an endorsement written on a document.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Examination" is:
e: Pariksha is an examination or test of candidates. Nirikshan is inspection, Satyapan is verification and Mulyaankan is evaluation or assessment.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Interest" (on money) is:
e: Byaj is the charge paid for the use of borrowed money, i.e., interest. Labh is profit, Kiraya is rent and Bhatta is an allowance.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Article" (of the Constitution) is:
e: A numbered provision of the Constitution is an Article, called Anuchhed. A Dhara is a section of an Act, an Adhyay a chapter and an Anusuchi a schedule.

q: The standard Hindi equivalent of the English administrative term "Section" (of an Act) is:
e: A numbered provision of an Act is a Section, called Dhara. The articles of the Constitution are Anuchhed, a chapter is Adhyay and a Parishisht an appendix.

q: The Gazette of India is published in:
e: The Gazette of India is published bilingually, in both Hindi and English, so that official notifications appear in the two versions side by side.

q: The Central Institute of Indian Languages, Mysuru was set up primarily for:

options.A: Coordinating the development of Indian languages
options.B: Conducting the Prabodh, Praveen and Pragya examinations

e: The Central Institute of Indian Languages, Mysuru, was set up primarily to coordinate the development of all Indian languages and to support language planning, research and training.

q: The Mahatma Gandhi Antarrashtriya Hindi Vishwavidyalaya (Mahatma Gandhi International Hindi University) is located at:
e: The Mahatma Gandhi Antarrashtriya Hindi Vishwavidyalaya, a central university devoted to Hindi, is located at Wardha in Maharashtra.

q: The Sahitya Akademi gives its awards for literary works in how many languages?
e: The Sahitya Akademi gives its awards in 24 languages - the 22 languages of the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution together with English and Rajasthani.

q: The Committee of Parliament on Official Language discharges its functions through how many sub-committees?
e: The Committee of Parliament on Official Language carries out its task of reviewing the progress of Hindi and inspecting offices through three sub-committees.

q: Under the Annual Programme for the progressive use of Hindi, at least what proportion of the amount spent on purchase of books for office libraries should be spent on Hindi books?
e: Under the Annual Programme for the progressive use of Hindi, offices must spend at least 50 per cent of the amount for purchase of books for their libraries on Hindi books.

q: The Tamil language was accorded the status of a 'classical language' by the Government of India in the year:
e: Tamil was the first language to be declared a classical language by the Government of India, receiving that status in 2004 in view of its ancient literature and heritage.

q: According to the Census of India, 2011, the seventh most widely spoken language (mother tongue) in India is:
e: In Census 2011, after Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Telugu, Tamil and Gujarati, Urdu stands seventh among the most widely spoken mother tongues in India.

q: In the year 2019, Hindi was included as one of the official languages of the courts of:
e: In 2019 Hindi was included as an official language of the courts of Abu Dhabi, helping the large Hindi-speaking workforce there to follow court proceedings.

q: The Devanagari script, in which Hindi is written, is also known as:
e: Devanagari, the script in which Hindi is written, is also simply called Nagari. Kaithi, Modi and Sharada are other traditional Indian scripts.

q: The language of the subordinate (district) courts in the State of Maharashtra is:
e: The language of the subordinate courts in Maharashtra is Marathi, the official language of the State, in which district-level court business is conducted.

q: The language of the subordinate (district) courts in the State of Punjab is:
e: The language of the subordinate courts in Punjab is Punjabi, the official language of the State, used for district-level judicial work.

q: The Braj Bhasha dialect belongs to which group of Hindi dialects?
e: Braj Bhasha, the classical language of Krishna devotional poetry, belongs to the Western Hindi group, along with Khari Boli, Kanauji, Bundeli and Haryanvi.

q: The Bagheli dialect belongs to which group of Hindi dialects?
e: Bagheli, spoken in the Baghelkhand region, belongs to the Eastern Hindi group, together with Awadhi and Chhattisgarhi.

q: The Magahi language belongs to which group of languages/dialects?
e: Magahi, spoken in the Magadh region of Bihar, belongs to the Bihari group of languages, along with Bhojpuri and Maithili.

q: The Kumaoni and Garhwali dialects belong to which group of Hindi dialects?
e: Kumaoni and Garhwali, spoken in the hill districts of Uttarakhand, together form the Pahari group of Hindi dialects.

q: The celebrated Hindi poem 'Jhansi ki Rani' was composed by:
e: The celebrated ballad 'Jhansi ki Rani', beginning with the praise of Rani Lakshmibai's valour, was composed by Subhadra Kumari Chauhan.

q: 'Priyapravas', regarded as the first epic poem (mahakavya) in Khari Boli Hindi, was written by:
e: 'Priyapravas' by Ayodhya Singh Upadhyay 'Hariaudh' is regarded as the first epic poem (mahakavya) written in Khari Boli Hindi.

q: The celebrated Hindi poem 'Bharat-Bharati' was written by:
e: 'Bharat-Bharati', the stirring poem on India's glorious past and fallen present that awakened national feeling, was written by Maithili Sharan Gupt.

q: 'Urvashi', the celebrated Hindi epic poem for which its author received the Jnanpith Award, was written by:
e: Ramdhari Singh Dinkar received the Jnanpith Award for 'Urvashi', his celebrated epic poem retelling the story of Pururava and Urvashi.

q: The celebrated Hindi play 'Andher Nagari' was written by:
e: 'Andher Nagari', the famous satirical play exposing misrule through the city where everything sells at one price, was written by Bharatendu Harishchandra.

q: The 'Hanuman Chalisa', the popular devotional hymn in praise of Lord Hanuman, was composed by:
e: The 'Hanuman Chalisa', forty verses of praise of Lord Hanuman recited by millions, was composed by Goswami Tulsidas, the author of the Ramcharitmanas.

q: The 'Bihari Satsai', a celebrated collection of couplets in Braj Bhasha, was composed by:
e: The 'Bihari Satsai', a collection of about seven hundred couplets in Braj Bhasha famed for their love imagery and wit, was composed by Bihari Lal.

q: The 'Tar Saptak' (1943), the anthology that heralded modern experimental poetry in Hindi, was edited by:
e: 'Tar Saptak' (1943), the anthology of seven poets that launched experimental modern poetry (Prayogvad) in Hindi, was edited by Agyeya.

q: The celebrated work 'Hindi Sahitya ka Itihas' (History of Hindi Literature) was written by:
e: Acharya Ramchandra Shukla's 'Hindi Sahitya ka Itihas' is the pioneering systematic history of Hindi literature, still a standard reference work.
